title: Ketia bar Shalom
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Avodah Zarah 10b relates that he was a great and honored minister in the Roman government. The emperor hated the Jews; he gathered all his ministers and said to them: “If someone has an abscess on his foot, should he cut it off and live, or leave it and suffer?” They said to him: “He should cut it off and live.” Ketia bar Shalom said to them: “First, you cannot [destroy] all of them … and furthermore, they will call you a truncated kingdom.” He said to him: “You have spoken well; but whoever defeats the king is thrown into a chamber filled with earth.” As they were taking him (to be killed), a certain noblewoman said to him: “Woe to the ship that goes without paying the tax” (you are going to be killed for Israel’s sake and you are not circumcised). He fell on the tip of his foreskin and cut it off, and commanded that all his property be given to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues … A heavenly voice went out and said: “Ketia bar Shalom is destined for the life of the world to come.”
Hyman suggests that possibly he was called Ketia (“cut off”) because he defeated the king by cutting himself, and called bar Shalom because he had life in the world to come.

notes.text: Saved Vilna Rashi Avodah Zarah10b explains לקמוניא חלילא as בית מלא עפר, a chamber filled with earth/dust; the old furnace/Rashi note is incorrect and withdrawn in the current edition. Saved Davidson English says a house full of ashes. The physical interpretations remain attributed; יוצר is read as יוצא and Hyman’s name etymology stays conjectural.

The complete inspected Avodah Zarah 10b narrative contains the kingdom argument, self-circumcision, bequest and heavenly voice. Rashi explicitly glosses the execution chamber as a house filled with earth; Davidson’s English gives ashes. The historical furnace gloss remains withdrawn, and Hyman’s proposed name etymology remains conjectural.
